141.title: Small groups
141.hook: Wesley's class meetings asked one question: how is it with your soul?
141.carry: how is it with your soul?
141.howItsDone: Many Christians belong to a small group that meets weekly in a home or at church to read the Bible, pray and talk honestly about their lives; Methodist class meetings and their question 'how is it with your soul?' are one historic model.

segments.voice: Yesterday: koinonia, sharing a common life, the first believers eating together from house to house. Your line was you weren't meant to do it alone. Who did you share a meal with? Day one hundred forty-one.
screen: `YOU WEREN'T MEANT TO DO IT ALONE.`

segments.voice: How are you? Fine. You? Good, busy. The exchange is so quick it barely counts as a question. Now step into a room of about a dozen people, farmers, miners, maids, shopkeepers, in eighteenth-century England, meeting on a weeknight. A leader goes around the circle, and to each person, he asks the same question. Not how are you. Not how's work. How is it with your soul? And each person has to answer. Honestly. In front of the others. Every single week. Today, the small group, and how a fundraising plan turned into a way of caring for souls.
screen: `FINE. YOU? GOOD, BUSY.` → `A DOZEN PEOPLE, ONE QUESTION.` → `HOW IS IT WITH YOUR SOUL?`

segments.voice: Small groups. Bristol, England, 1742. The Methodists, the movement led by John Wesley, owe money on their new meeting house. Someone suggests a practical fix: divide the members into groups of about twelve, and have a leader collect a penny a week from each. Simple. But the leaders, going door to door for their pennies, keep finding out things. Things like a man drinking again, or a family that can't eat. Wesley saw what was happening and turned it into the heart of the movement. The class meeting was born. Once a week, each class met with its leader. They sang, they prayed, and the leader asked each one about their life with God. The question tradition remembers them by is today's line: how is it with your soul? The classes could do something a sermon couldn't. You can hide in a crowd of a thousand. You can't hide in a circle of twelve people who know your name. Jesus had said something that makes small numbers matter. In the King James Bible: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Two or three is enough. The idea has spread far beyond Methodism. Today there are home groups, cell groups, Bible studies around kitchen tables, Catholic small faith communities. All of them share the same bet: that people change less from being taught at and more from being known. Wesley's version started with pennies.
screen: `BRISTOL, 1742: A PENNY A WEEK.` · `THE LEADERS KEEP FINDING THINGS.` · `YOU CAN'T HIDE IN A CIRCLE OF TWELVE.` · `CHANGED BY BEING KNOWN.` · then, large: `WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. First, ask the question of yourself. How is it with your soul? Not your calendar or your inbox. Your soul, whatever that word means to you right now. Let the honest answer come, even if it's tired, or muddled, or better than you expected. Sit with it. Then think of one person you could ask, really ask, how they are. Someone who'd get past fine if they knew you meant it. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Small groups. A dozen people, meeting weekly, known by name. Wesley's class meetings turned a penny collection into honest care.
Your line: how is it with your soul? Today, ask someone how they really are, and wait past the first fine. Day one hundred forty-one.

options: collect the penny anyway: rules are rules.

142.title: Bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2)
142.hook: carrying each other's loads is how the law of Christ is kept
142.howItsDone: Many churches organize meals, visits, rides and prayer for members going through illness, grief or hardship, and many Christians take Galatians 6:2 as a description of what church should be.

segments.voice: Yesterday: small groups, and Wesley's weekly question. Your line was how is it with your soul? Did anyone get past fine with you? Day one hundred forty-two.

Moving day. You've boxed up your whole life, and the couch is at the bottom of three flights of stairs. Alone, it's impossible. You'd wreck your back and the wall. Then two friends show up, one on each end, and suddenly it's awkward, funny and done in ten minutes. The same weight, split, becomes something else. Paul, writing a letter to the churches in Galatia, reaches for exactly that picture. He's been arguing for five chapters about rules and freedom, and then, near the end, he gives the churches an instruction that sounds a lot like moving day. Today, a short line that turns out to be a whole way of living.
screen: `THREE FLIGHTS, ONE COUCH.` → `TWO FRIENDS SHOW UP.` → `THE SAME WEIGHT, SPLIT.`

segments.voice: Bear one another's burdens. Here's the whole verse, in the King James Bible: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." Notice what Paul does there. The Galatians have been arguing about which laws Christians must keep. And Paul says: you want a law? Here's the law of Christ. Carry each other. It's not a new rulebook. It's love you can lift. Now, a puzzle. Three verses later, Paul seems to say the opposite: "For every man shall bear his own burden." Wait. Which is it? The answer is in the Greek. In verse two, the word for burdens means heavy weights, crushing loads, the kind nobody should carry alone. In verse five, it's a different word: a load or a pack, which some readers picture as the kit a soldier carries on a march. Your own daily load. So Paul is saying both. Carry your own pack. Do your own work, own your own choices. And when someone is crushed by a weight too heavy for one person, a grief, an illness, a debt, a failure, get under it with them. Both at once. The verse just before says who does the lifting: if someone is caught in a fault, restore them gently, remembering you could be next. It's easy to hear bear one another's burdens as fix other people. It isn't. You don't take the weight away. You stand under it with them. Christians have lived this in casseroles after funerals, rides to chemotherapy, rent paid quietly, friends who sit with you on the worst night and say almost nothing. The law of Christ looks a lot like showing up with your end of the couch.
screen: `THE LAW OF CHRIST: CARRY EACH OTHER.` · `TWO WORDS FOR BURDEN.` · `A CRUSHING WEIGHT, AND A DAILY PACK.` · `STAND UNDER IT WITH THEM.` · then, large: `BEAR YE ONE ANOTHER'S BURDENS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. First, notice your own pack: what you're carrying today that's simply yours to carry. Just name it. Then think of someone you know under a heavy weight right now. Illness, grief, money, a child in trouble, a job that's crushing them. Picture them for a minute. Don't try to fix it in your head. Just ask: where is one corner of this I could lift? A meal. A ride. An hour of childcare. A text that says I'm here. If you pray, you can hold them before God. The bell holds the time.
Bear one another's burdens. Paul's summary of the law of Christ: get under the crushing weight with someone.
Your line: carry each other. Today, help carry one load, one corner of someone else's heavy thing. Day one hundred forty-two.

143.title: He withdrew (Luke 5:16)
143.hook: even at his busiest, Jesus slipped away to lonely places to pray
143.howItsDone: Many Christians follow Jesus's habit of withdrawing by keeping a daily time of solitary prayer, going on retreats at monasteries or retreat centers, and setting aside quiet days away from work.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bear one another's burdens, two words for burden, and the law of Christ. Your line was carry each other. Whose load did you help lift? Now the week turns from together to alone. Day one hundred forty-three.

Some days the phone won't stop. Messages, calls, people who need something, all of it urgent, all of it real. Luke describes days like that for Jesus. He's just healed a man with leprosy, and the news has gone everywhere. Crowds are pouring in from the towns. People who are sick, people who are desperate, people who want to hear him. The need is enormous and it's growing by the hour. If there was ever a moment to stay, to keep going, to not waste a single minute, this is it. And Luke tells us, in one short sentence, what he did instead. It's so quick you could read right past it. Today: he withdrew.
screen: `THE NEWS HAS GONE EVERYWHERE.` → `THE CROWDS KEEP GROWING.` → `AND THEN, ONE SHORT SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: He withdrew. Here are the two verses together, in the King James Bible. First the pressure: "But so much the more went there a fame abroad of him: and great multitudes came together to hear, and to be healed by him of their infirmities." Then the turn: "And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed." That's it. No explanation. No apology to the crowd. But look closer at the Greek, because the grammar tells a story. Luke doesn't say he withdrew once. The form he uses describes something ongoing, repeated. A fair way to put it: he would keep slipping away. Many readers hear a habit here, not an emergency. And where does he go? The wilderness, lonely places, deserted places. Not a better office. Somewhere empty. Luke keeps catching Jesus praying: at his baptism, all night before choosing the twelve, on the mountain where he's transfigured, in the garden at the end. In Mark, when his friends come back from their work with no time even to eat, he tells them: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." Here's what's surprising. The withdrawing never replaced the crowds. He came back. In Luke's very next story, a paralyzed man is lowered through a roof, and Jesus is right there, teaching and healing. The quiet didn't take him away from people. It seems to be how he could keep giving to them. Christians have built whole ways of life on this rhythm: monks and nuns in the desert, retreats, a quiet hour before the day begins. Not as an escape. As the way back in.
screen: `THE CROWDS GROW BY THE HOUR.` · `HE WOULD KEEP SLIPPING AWAY.` · `LONELY PLACES, NOT A BETTER OFFICE.` · `THE QUIET WAS THE WAY BACK IN.` · then, large: `HE WITHDREW HIMSELF INTO THE WILDERNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Right now, for these two minutes, withdraw. Turn your phone face down, or put it in another room if you can. If there's a door, close it. If you're on a bus, close your eyes. Let the crowd of your day, the messages, the needs, the noise, wait on the other side. Nothing is on fire that can't wait two minutes. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can simply be with God, with no list. If you don't, just be here, unreachable, for a little while. The bell holds the time.
He withdrew. Even when the crowds were largest, Jesus kept slipping away to lonely places to pray, and then came back.
Your line: withdraw to return. Today, find five minutes alone, no phone, and then go back to your people. Day one hundred forty-three.

144.title: The quiet time
144.hook: many Christians keep a morning quiet time: a Bible, a notebook, a coffee
144.howItsDone: Many Christians keep a daily quiet time, often in the morning, reading a short Bible passage, writing in a journal and praying; others pray morning prayer from the daily office or say set morning prayers before icons at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday: he withdrew. Even with crowds at the door, Jesus kept slipping away to pray. Your line was withdraw to return. Did you find five minutes alone? Day one hundred forty-four.

Six-fifteen in the morning. The house is still dark. A kettle clicks off. Someone sits at the kitchen table with a mug in one hand and, in front of them, three things: a Bible with a cracked spine, a cheap notebook, and a pen. No phone. Not yet. They read a few verses. They sit. They write a line or two. Maybe a name they're worried about. Maybe a question. Twenty minutes, sometimes ten, sometimes five. Then the day comes crashing in, kids, email, traffic. Christians in many places start their mornings something like this. In evangelical churches, it has a name. Today, the quiet time.
screen: `SIX-FIFTEEN, STILL DARK.` → `A BIBLE, A NOTEBOOK, A MUG.` → `THEN THE DAY COMES IN.`

segments.voice: The quiet time. The phrase is fairly recent, at home in evangelical churches and student groups. But the habit is ancient. The Psalms are full of mornings. In the King James Bible, Psalm five says: "My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up." Direct my prayer, and look up. The Hebrew word there for direct can mean to lay something out in order, like wood arranged for a fire, or a table set for a meal. The psalmist sets out the morning's prayer, then watches for an answer. And the book of Lamentations, a book of grief over a fallen city, still manages to say of God's mercies: "They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." New every morning. That's the logic of first thing. You haven't failed at anything yet. The day hasn't told you who you are. So what actually happens in a quiet time? It varies, and that's fine. Some read a short passage, often following a plan. Some write in a journal: what the verse said, what's on their mind, a prayer list. Catholics and Anglicans may pray morning prayer from the daily office, with psalms set for each day. Orthodox Christians may stand before icons at home and say the morning prayers. Some just sit in silence with coffee. The common thread is not the method. It's the order. Before the world gets its say, a little quiet gets the first word. Nobody promises it will feel profound. Plenty of mornings are sleepy and blank. People keep it anyway, the way you keep a friendship: by showing up.
screen: `A MODERN NAME, AN ANCIENT HABIT.` · `IN THE MORNING WILL I DIRECT MY PRAYER.` · `READ, WRITE, SIT, OR PRAY THE OFFICE.` · `BEFORE THE WORLD GETS ITS SAY.` · then, large: `NEW EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you have a notebook nearby, open it. If not, a scrap of paper, or the notes on your phone with everything else turned off. Breathe. At the top, write today's date. Then write one line: what's on your mind right now, honestly. Then sit with it. Don't fix it, don't polish it. If you pray, you can write a name or a need, and offer it. If you don't, just let the page hold what you're carrying. When you're ready, write one more line if it comes. The bell holds the time.
The quiet time. A small daily window, often in the morning: a few verses, a notebook, some silence, before the day begins.
Your line: first thing, a little quiet. Tomorrow morning, before the phone, sit with a notebook for three minutes. Day one hundred forty-four.

145.title: Be still (Psalm 46:10)
145.hook: be still, and know that I am God
145.howItsDone: Many Christians pray Psalm 46 in times of fear or crisis, and some use 'be still, and know that I am God' as a short prayer in silent or contemplative prayer, repeated slowly with the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the quiet time, a notebook and a mug before the day begins. Your line was first thing, a little quiet. Did the quiet get the first word this morning? Day one hundred forty-five.

You've probably seen these words somewhere. On a mug. A throw pillow. A calm lake photo on someone's wall, with a single line in soft script: be still, and know that I am God. It looks like a spa brochure. Gentle, peaceful, a little sleepy. So here's the surprise. The psalm that line comes from doesn't picture a quiet lake. It pictures the ground giving way, and a war. Mountains sliding into the sea. Nations raging. Kingdoms toppling. Bows, spears and chariots. And right in the middle of all that noise, God speaks two words. Today, be still, and why it's much stronger than it looks on the pillow.
screen: `ON A MUG, BY A CALM LAKE.` → `BUT THE PSALM IS LOUD.` → `EARTHQUAKE AND WAR.`

segments.voice: Be still. Psalm forty-six opens like this, in the King James Bible: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." Then it gets loud. "Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea." The waters roar, the nations rage, kingdoms are moved, the earth melts. Then the psalm turns: God "maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder." And only then, verse ten: "Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth." Now the Hebrew. Be still is one word, harpu. Its root means to let go, to sink down, to let your hands drop. Like soldiers told to lower their weapons. Like someone who's been gripping the wheel for hours finally unclenching. So it's less relax, more stop. Drop it. Let go. Some scholars think it's spoken first to the warring nations: stop fighting, and know who's God. Others hear it spoken to the frightened people inside the city. Plenty of readers hear both. Either way, stillness here is not calm scenery. It's what happens when you stop trying to hold up the mountains yourself. Martin Luther loved this psalm; his great hymn A Mighty Fortress Is Our God grew out of it. And Jews and Christians alike have prayed it in wartime, in plague and in grief. The pillow isn't wrong. It's just missing the earthquake. The stillness is meant for the moment everything is shaking.
screen: `A VERY PRESENT HELP IN TROUBLE.` · `MOUNTAINS INTO THE SEA.` · `HARPU — LET GO, DROP YOUR HANDS.` · `STILLNESS IN THE EARTHQUAKE.` · then, large: `BE STILL, AND KNOW THAT I AM GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Two minutes of stillness. Sit, and let your hands rest open on your knees or in your lap. Notice where you're gripping: your jaw, your shoulders, your hands. Let each one drop, the way the Hebrew word suggests. Think of the thing that's shaking in your life right now. Don't solve it. Just let go of holding it up for two minutes. If you pray, you can say the line slowly, once: be still, and know that I am God. Then stay still. If you don't pray, just stay. The bell holds the time.
Be still. In Hebrew, harpu: let go, drop your hands. Said in the middle of an earthquake and a war.
Your line: be still, and know. Today, when something shakes you, drop your hands for three breaths before you grab for it. Day one hundred forty-five.

146.title: Why fast (Matthew 6:16–18)
146.hook: Jesus says when you fast, not if: quietly, without a gloomy face
146.howItsDone: Many Christians fast by skipping meals or certain foods on set days or seasons, spending the time in prayer, and many give up a comfort instead when fasting from food isn't safe for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: be still, harpu, let go and drop your hands, said in the middle of an earthquake. Your line was be still, and know. When did you drop your hands? Day one hundred forty-six.

Skipping lunch is easy to announce. "Oh, I'm not eating today." A little sigh. A small pause, in case anyone wants to ask why. Some people do their diet or their detox out loud. Now go to Jesus on a hillside in Galilee, teaching a crowd, and he gets to fasting. He doesn't explain it. He doesn't argue for it. He assumes it. Not if you fast. When. And then, just as he did with giving earlier in the same sermon, he goes straight for the performance. He describes people who go around looking hungry on purpose, faces smudged and gloomy, so everyone can tell how holy they are. And he says: do the opposite. Today's word is the practice he's talking about.
screen: `I'M NOT EATING TODAY. SIGH.` → `NOT IF YOU FAST. WHEN.` → `THE GLOOMY FACE.`

segments.voice: Fasting. Going without food, or some food, for a time, for the sake of prayer. Here's what Jesus says in Matthew six, in the King James Bible: "Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast." Then: "But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret." Wash your face. Do your hair. Look normal. The same pattern as giving in secret, a few lines earlier. Of those who fast for show, Jesus says: "They have their reward." Jesus himself fasted. Before his ministry began, the gospels say he spent forty days in the wilderness and was hungry afterward. Moses fasted on the mountain. Elijah walked forty days on the strength of one meal. Esther asked her people to fast before she risked her life. It's woven all through the Bible, and Jesus stands inside that tradition. So why would anyone choose to be hungry? Christians give a few reasons. Hunger clears the head; it reminds you that you're a body, dependent, not in control. Every pang becomes a small bell calling you back to prayer. That's today's line: hunger can pray. Fasting also makes room: the time and money you'd spend on food can go to someone else. And it's a way of saying, with your whole body, that you mean it. A caution many churches give: fasting is not a diet, and it's not for everyone. People who are pregnant, ill or recovering from an eating disorder are usually told not to fast from food at all. Many choose to fast from something else instead.
screen: `GOING WITHOUT, FOR PRAYER.` · `WASH THY FACE. LOOK NORMAL.` · `MOSES, ELIJAH, ESTHER, JESUS.` · `EVERY PANG A SMALL BELL.` · then, large: `WHEN YE FAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Not a fast today, just a small taste of the idea. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small comfort you reach for without thinking: the second coffee, the snack at three, the scroll before bed, the sugar in your tea. Pick one. Just one, for today. Now think ahead to the moment later today when you'll reach for it and it won't be there. Instead of the thing, there will be a small ache. If you pray, you can let that ache become a short prayer. If you don't, let it be a moment of noticing. The bell holds the time.
Fasting. Going without for a while, for the sake of prayer. Jesus says when, not if, and quietly, with a washed face.
Your line: hunger can pray. Today, skip one small comfort, tell nobody, and let the little ache point somewhere. Day one hundred forty-six.

147.title: Fasting across the church
147.hook: Orthodox Christians fast most Wednesdays and Fridays; Catholics fast in Lent; many Protestants fast for a cause
147.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians fast from meat and dairy on most Wednesdays and Fridays and during several seasons; Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and avoid meat on Lenten Fridays; many Protestants keep Lent or fast together for a particular need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fasting, and Jesus saying when you fast, not if, with a washed face. Your line was hunger can pray. What small comfort did you skip? Day one hundred forty-seven.

What's for dinner on a fast day? It depends whose kitchen you're in. A Greek grandmother is cooking beans and greens in water, no meat, no cheese, no olive oil even, as she has on Wednesdays and Fridays for most of her life. A Catholic family is having fish sticks, because it's a Friday in Lent. segments.voice: Fasting across the church. Start early. An ancient Christian handbook called the Didache tells Christians to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays. Tradition links Friday with the day Jesus died, and Wednesday with the day he was betrayed. That weekly rhythm is still alive. Orthodox churches keep a long fasting calendar. On most Wednesdays and Fridays of the year, through Great Lent before Easter and in several other seasons, Orthodox Christians set aside meat and dairy, and often fish, wine and olive oil. It's done in community, and people are told to adjust for health and circumstance. Catholic rules today center on a few days. On Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, adults fast: one full meal and two small ones. On Fridays in Lent, no meat, which is why parish fish fries turn up in Lent. Giving up something personal for Lent is a familiar Catholic custom too. Protestant churches vary widely. Anglicans, Lutherans and Methodists often keep Lent. The early Methodists fasted on Fridays, and John Wesley urged it. Some evangelical and Pentecostal churches call a fast for a specific need: a sick friend, a decision, a new year. Some follow the pattern of Daniel, who said: "I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine in my mouth." The rules differ. Each tradition is clearing something away, food, time, a habit, to make space. Space for prayer, for hunger to remind you, and for others. Whether you keep a calendar of fasts or none, the idea underneath is the same: make space.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Picture this month's calendar. Now pick one day on it. Maybe a Wednesday or a Friday, the Didache's days. Ask what you could fast from that day. It doesn't have to be food. It could be meat, or sugar, or coffee. It could be your phone after dinner, or streaming, or shopping. Choose one. Notice how it feels to decide in advance. If you pray, you can offer that day to God now. If you don't, simply mark it as a day to make space. The bell holds the time.
